facts.statement: The gyrification index quantifies how much the surface of a mammal's brain is folded.
Among mammals, those with more folded brains tend to be physically larger than those with smoother brains.
The human brain has a folding index that is comparable to that of a horse, though slightly higher.
Rodents typically possess the least folded brains among mammals.
Despite the general trend, certain larger rodent species do exhibit folded brain surfaces.
The human brain contains a greater amount of association, sensory, and motor cortex compared to smaller mammals like rats and cats.
In humans, the cerebral cortex makes up a larger proportion of the brain than it does in many other mammal species.
All mammalian brains, including those of humans and rats, share a six-layered cerebral cortex along with structures like the hippocampus and amygdala.
Relative to body size, the human cerebral cortex is significantly larger than that of most other mammals, and humans possess a highly developed visual system.
The average human brain weighs between 1.3 and 1.5 kilograms.
In general, an animal's brain size correlates with its overall body size.
Across all mammal orders, brain weight scales with body size according to a power law with an exponent of roughly 0.75.
For their body size, primates possess brains that are five to ten times larger than the general mammalian average.
As brain size increases in a species, the proportion of the brain volume occupied by the cortex also increases.
In species with the largest brains, including humans, the majority of the brain's volume is composed of cortex.
The human encephalization quotient, a measure of brain size relative to body size, ranges from 7.4 to 7.8.
Some researchers argue that intelligence is more strongly linked to the number of cortical neurons and connection speed than to total brain size.

en.text: Both human and rat brains share a fundamental architecture, featuring a six-layered cerebral cortex (the outer neural sheet) alongside structures like the hippocampus and amygdala.
While rodents typically possess the least folded brains among mammals, the human brain exhibits a gyrification index (a measure of surface folding) comparable to that of a horse.
In contrast to the rat, the human cerebral cortex constitutes a larger proportion of the total brain volume and contains a greater amount of association, sensory, and motor cortex.
As brain size increases in a species, the proportion of volume occupied by the cortex also increases, meaning that in humans the majority of the brain's volume is composed of cortex.

es.text: Los cerebros humano y de rata comparten una arquitectura fundamental, caracterizada por una corteza cerebral de seis capas (la hoja neuronal externa) junto a estructuras como el hipocampo y la amígdala.

Si bien los roedores suelen tener los cerebros menos plegados entre los mamíferos, el cerebro humano presenta un índice de girificación (una medida del plegamiento de la superficie) comparable al de un caballo.
A diferencia de la rata, la corteza cerebral humana constituye una proporción mayor del volumen total del cerebro y contiene una mayor cantidad de corteza de asociación, sensorial y motora.

A medida que aumenta el tamaño del cerebro en una especie, también lo hace la proporción de volumen ocupada por la corteza, lo que significa que en los humanos la mayor parte del volumen cerebral está compuesta por corteza.

facts.statement: In rodents, the brain grows in size more quickly than its neuron count, leading to lower neuronal density and larger average neuron size as the brain gets bigger.
As rodent brains grow, the number of non-neuronal cells increases more than the number of neurons, causing the ratio of glia to neurons to rise.
Unlike rodents, primate brains grow in size proportionally to their neuron count, maintaining stable neuronal density and a constant ratio of non-neuronal to neuronal cells.
A tenfold increase in neuron number leads to a 35-fold increase in rodent brain size, whereas the same increase in primates results in only an 11-fold increase in brain size.
Primate brains pack more neurons into the same volume than rodent brains, resulting in higher neuronal densities.
In rodents, neuronal density drops as the brain gets bigger, whereas in primates it stays constant, widening the neuron count gap between the two groups as brain size increases.
The human cerebral cortex makes up 82% of the brain's mass but contains just 19% of its neurons, a proportion similar to that seen in rodents and other primates.

As brains grow larger in both rodents and primates, the number of neurons in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum increases much faster than the number in the brainstem, diencephalon, and basal ganglia.
Scaling rules for both rodents and primates predict that the cerebral cortex's mass expands relative to the whole brain, a trend not observed in the small rodent species studied.
The human cerebral cortex has 16 billion neurons, slightly fewer than expected for a 1.5 kg primate, while the human cerebellum has 69 billion neurons, matching or slightly exceeding expectations.
The number of neurons spanning the depth of the cortex is generally constant across species, but primates have 2.5 times more neurons in visual area 17.
GABAergic interneurons make up no more than 15% of cortical neurons in rats, whereas they can reach 34–44% in certain layers of the human brain.
Human dendritic spines have twice the volume of those found in the mouse somatosensory cortex.
The necks of dendritic spines are approximately 30% longer in humans than in mice.
Double bouquet cells, which are abundant in primates, do not appear to exist in rodents.
Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) interneurons are relatively few in the rat cortex and are most abundant in layers II and III.
Most TH interneurons in the rat cortex are GABAergic, while only about half are GABAergic in the human neocortex.

en.text: While rodent brains expand in size faster than their neuron count, primate brains grow proportionally to their neuronal numbers, maintaining stable density.
Consequently, the ratio of glia to neurons rises in rodents as they grow, whereas primates keep this ratio constant.
This difference means primates pack more neurons into the same volume, widening the neuron count gap as brain size increases.
In the cortex, GABAergic interneurons make up no more than 15% of neurons in rats, but they can reach 34–44% in certain human layers.
Furthermore, human dendritic spines have twice the volume of those in the mouse somatosensory cortex, with necks approximately 30% longer.
Double bouquet cells, which are abundant in primates, do not appear to exist in rodents.

es.text: Mientras que los cerebros de los roedores aumentan de tamaño más rápido que su número de neuronas, los de los primados crecen en proporción a su cantidad neuronal, manteniendo una densidad estable.
En consecuencia, la proporción de glía respecto a las neuronas aumenta en los roedores a medida que crecen, mientras que los primados mantienen esta proporción constante.
Esta diferencia significa que los primados alojan más neuronas en el mismo volumen, lo que amplía la brecha en el número de neuronas a medida que aumenta el tamaño del cerebro.
En la corteza, las interneuronas GABAérgicas representan como máximo el 15% de las neuronas en la rata, pero pueden alcanzar entre el 34% y el 44% en ciertas capas humanas.
Además, las espinas dendríticas humanas tienen el doble de volumen que las de la corteza somatosensorial del ratón, con cuellos aproximadamente un 30% más largos.
Las células de doble ramillete, abundantes en los primados, no parecen existir en los roedores.
